title: Nights in the Gardens of Spain (Noches en los jardines de España)
hook: Three Andalusian gardens at night, for a piano that blends into the orchestra like a guitar heard across the dark.

painting.title: Gardens of the Generalife
painting.collection: Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya, Barcelona
painting.pairingNote: The cypress walk of the Generalife in Granada, painted in 1909, the year Falla began the piano nocturnes that grew into this work; its first movement is set in the same gardens.

facts: Falla began the music in Paris in 1909 as a set of nocturnes for solo piano. The pianist Ricardo Viñes suggested turning them into a work for piano and orchestra. When the First World War broke out Falla returned to Spain, and he finished it in 1915. It is dedicated to Viñes.
The first performance was at the Teatro Real in Madrid on 9 April 1916, with José Cubiles at the piano and Enrique Fernández Arbós conducting the Orquesta Sinfónica de Madrid.

Falla called it “symphonic impressions for piano and orchestra”, not a concerto. The piano part is brilliant but rarely dominates: it is woven into the orchestra, often imitating the strummed and plucked sounds of a guitar. The colours owe much to Debussy and Ravel, Falla’s friends in Paris.

The tunes are not folk songs, but they are built from the rhythms, scales and ornaments of Andalusian music. Falla wrote that the work “has no pretensions to being descriptive; it is merely expressive”, and that “melancholy and mystery” have their part, as well as the sounds of festivals and dances.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a night in the gardens of the Alhambra (I), a dance heard from far away (II), and a fiesta in the hills of Córdoba that fades into the dark (III).

movements.heading: En el Generalife
movements.title: En el Generalife (In the Generalife)
movements.summary: The Generalife is the summer garden of the Moorish kings, on the hill beside the Alhambra in Granada, full of fountains, cypresses and jasmine. The music begins in a hush, with rustling strings and a melody that turns around a few notes. The piano enters with quick, glittering figures, and the music slowly gathers into a passionate climax before sinking back into the night.

mainIdeas.name: The night theme
mainIdeas.description: a narrow, winding melody that circles a few notes, in the woodwinds and strings over a soft, rustling accompaniment.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s figures
mainIdeas.description: rapid repeated notes and ripples that sound like a guitar or like water.

mainIdeas.name: The climax
mainIdeas.description: the same winding melody, broadened and loud, with the piano in heavy chords.

stops.hear: Very quiet, trembling strings and a harp; a melody winds around a few notes
stops.happening: Night in the garden. The opening idea, built from Andalusian ornaments

stops.hear: The piano enters with quick, crystal-clear figures over the hazy strings
stops.happening: The piano’s first entry, like a guitar heard in the dark

stops.hear: Piano and orchestra trade the winding melody; short patterns repeat and interlock
stops.happening: The patterns some hear as the geometric tilework of the Alhambra

stops.hear: The music swells; the whole orchestra takes up the melody, the piano hammers chords
Calm returns; the piano plays alone, decorating the melody
A second, shorter surge in the full orchestra

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The sounds thin out; soft chords, a last ripple in the piano

notice: Listen to how seldom the piano plays a tune of its own. Mostly it adds colour: shimmering repeated notes, rippling figures, strummed chords. That is why Falla would not call the work a concerto.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Alicia de Larrocha (1923–2009), born in Barcelona, was best known for her recordings of Spanish music, Falla’s included. This version, with the London Philharmonic and the Spanish conductor Rafael Frühbeck de Burgos, was made in July 1983 at Walthamstow Assembly Hall in London. On the Spotify album the three movements are tracks 1–3.

movements.heading: Danza lejana
movements.title: Danza lejana (A Distant Dance)
movements.summary: A dance heard from far away, in a garden that Falla does not name. It begins softly, with a swaying rhythm, and the piano takes up the dance tune with Andalusian turns and flourishes. The dance comes closer and grows more insistent, and then, without a break, it runs straight into the last movement.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a lilting, swaying rhythm, first in the orchestra, soft and distant.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s tune
mainIdeas.description: ornamented with quick turns and trills, in the manner of Spanish song.

stops.hear: A soft, swaying dance rhythm in the strings and woodwinds, as if from far off
The piano takes the dance tune, with quick ornaments and strummed chords
The dance grows louder and more insistent; the orchestra fills out
A quieter, more mysterious passage, with soft piano figures

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: The music builds and does not stop: it runs on into the next movement
stops.happening: The bridge to the finale, played without a break

notice: Notice how the end of the movement does not close. Falla links the second and third movements, so that the distant dance turns directly into the fiesta.

movements.heading: En los jardines de la Sierra de Córdoba
movements.title: En los jardines de la Sierra de Córdoba (In the Gardens of the Sierra de Córdoba)
movements.summary: A fiesta in the gardens of the hills outside Córdoba. Loud, rhythmic outbursts from the whole orchestra alternate with long, singing passages for the piano and strings, some of them as plaintive as flamenco song. After the last climax the celebration does not end with a bang: the music fades into a calm, quiet close.

mainIdeas.name: The fiesta
mainIdeas.description: hammered rhythms and strummed chords in piano and orchestra.

mainIdeas.name: The lament
mainIdeas.description: a long, ornamented melody that wails and turns like *cante jondo*, the “deep song” of Andalusia.

mainIdeas.name: The close
mainIdeas.description: slow, tender music for piano and strings.

stops.hear: A burst of energy: hammered chords and driving rhythms from the orchestra and the piano
The piano strikes chords in fast, rolling strokes, like a flamenco guitarist
stops.happening: Guitar strumming, [[rasgueado|rasgueado]], imitated on the piano

stops.hear: A long, wailing melody with twisting ornaments
stops.happening: A song in the style of *cante jondo*

stops.hear: Fiesta and song alternate; harsh, loud interruptions from the full orchestra
A broad, warm melody for piano and strings
stops.happening: A romance in the middle of the night

stops.hear: The orchestra builds to its biggest climax, the piano pounding beneath
The music slows and softens; piano and strings alone

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: A few quiet, glowing chords

notice: Listen for the moment after the last climax when the energy drains away. Falla ends a festival piece quietly, with “melancholy and mystery” having the last word.

threads.title: Gardens, not maps
threads.body: Falla insisted the music expresses rather than describes: the scent and mood of gardens at night, not a story or a tour.

threads.title: The guitar inside the piano
threads.body: In every movement the piano imitates the guitar: plucked repeated notes, strummed chords, rolling strokes. The real guitar never appears.

threads.title: Granada
threads.body: The first movement looks at the Generalife from afar; a few years later, in 1921, Falla went to live in Granada, below the Alhambra, and stayed for almost twenty years.
